Thought: Careful, heavily hedged evaluation paper. The controlled design (fixed papers, fixed model, fixed audit, fixed pre-split fact lists, symmetric completion rule) is genuinely good methodology and the within-paper full-text-hiding experiment is the cleanest result (79.8% vs 36.1%, 45/0/1). But the headline conclusion (access, not strategy, limits agreement with curators who read full papers) is acknowledged by the authors themselves to be expected, and the between-strategy differences are around 0-2 points, comparable to the 1.0-point replicate-noise half-width. Everything, including the 'supplied text states the fact' judgement on which Table 2 rests, is done by one model family with zero human validation; for a benchmark contribution this is the central gap. Reference covers only ~24% of what a draft says and is variant-centred ClinVar text. Single proprietary model with no seed control; strategies are in-house implementations. Domain is narrow for ICLR and the writing is extremely dense. Figures and tables are consistent with the text (checked Fig 2 counts, Fig 3 totals 1,837+4,282+379=6,498, Table 1/2 values). Leaning reject, persuadable with human validation and a second model family.
Summary: The paper builds a controlled benchmark for evidence-grounded knowledge-base writing from 100 OMIM phenotype entries (2-12 references each; 515 papers, 19% open-access full text). Each entry is drafted from its header and exactly the papers its curators cited (causal gene withheld) by one model (Claude Opus 5.5) under several generation strategies: direct long-context reading, an agentic curator with read/search tools, an evidence-graph extract-then-write pipeline, a case-table-first pipeline, recall-then-verify, a memory-only control, and three add-ons (second-hand evidence, reconciled case database, learned curation guide). All drafts go through the same claim-level audit and are scored on a primary endpoint, 'OMIM facts conveyed': coverage of fixed fact lists split once from OMIM allelic-variant descriptions deposited in ClinVar. Main findings: hiding full text of the same papers lowers coverage from 79.8% to 36.1%; on facts the supplied text (model-judged) states, three reading strategies convey 93.6-94.4% and on unstated facts 5.5-6.9%; direct reading, agentic curator and evidence graph are within ~0.7 points, case table first is behind by 1.9 points (8.4 on facts stated in full-text papers), memory-based strategies are far behind. The paper also reports measurement lessons (symmetric handling of safety-stopped replies, fixed fact lists, replicate noise), an audit planted-error test, a contamination check by entry creation date, and a matched ablation of the extract-then-write pipelines.
Strengths: Careful experimental control: same papers, same model, same guards, same audit and the same pre-split fact lists for every strategy, so the generation strategy is the only manipulated variable. Fixing the fact list once, without sight of any draft, avoids denominators that adapt to each draft (and the paper shows the afresh-split variant inflates levels by 2-5 points).

The within-paper access manipulation (hiding full text of the same 91 papers and rewriting from abstracts, scored on the same 2,120 facts, no arm repaired) is a clean causal estimate of how much access bounds agreement (+43.7 points, 45 entries higher, none lower), complemented by missed-fact attribution and conveyed-fact provenance analyses.

Unusually honest statistical reporting: paired bootstrap intervals over entries, better/worse/tie counts, sign tests, an intention-to-treat sensitivity analysis, replicate-noise yardsticks from three replicates on 30 entries, and explicit discussion of a corrected analysis (asymmetric completion rule) that had produced a spurious 2.1-point difference. This measurement lesson is useful beyond the domain.
Completion (safety-filter stops) is treated as an outcome rather than silently excluded, with a principled rule for one-call vs per-paper strategies.

Contamination is addressed with a memory-only control analysed by creation era and a held-out set of entries created in 2026; the memory-only control drops to ~6-7% coverage on the newest entries, while the reading strategies' ordering holds.

The matched ablation separates representation from incidental settings (extraction effort, rule-based synopsis terms) and shows much of case table first's deficit is due to extraction effort, a good example of not blaming a representation prematurely.

Claims are carefully scoped throughout (regime of 2-12 references, inputs that fit one prompt, one model), and limitations are listed explicitly; the per-entry release of drafts, verdicts and scores is valuable.
Weaknesses: No human validation of any judgement. The audit verdicts, the fact splitting, the present/partly/absent fact matching, the variant-name judge and, crucially, the 'supplied text states this fact' judgement that underlies Table 2 and the central 'access bounds agreement' argument are all made by the same model family that wrote the drafts. Given known self-preference effects (which the paper cites), a benchmark contribution needs at least a small curator- or expert-annotated sample to estimate judge agreement and calibrate the endpoint. Run-to-run judge variation (Appendix E) measures consistency, not validity.

Possible circularity in the 'stated facts' restriction: facts the model judges to be stated in the text (with a verified quote) are plausibly those the same model finds easy to locate and convey, so 93-94% coverage on that subset may partly reflect agreement between two passes of the same model rather than near-complete reading. A human-labelled subset, or a judge from a different model family, would address this.

The main conclusion is, as the authors acknowledge, expected: curators wrote from full papers, so drafts from abstracts convey less. The added value is the effect size within this setting, which is a modest scientific contribution for ICLR. The between-strategy differences (0-2 points) are of the same order as the replicate noise (half-width 1.0 point over 93 entries), so the comparison mostly yields nulls; the regime tested (2-12 references, everything fits in one prompt) is exactly where long-context direct reading is expected to be hard to beat, so the paper says little about when extraction or agentic designs would matter.

The reference is narrow and indirect: variant-centred OMIM allelic-variant paragraphs in ClinVar, not the phenotype entries' narrative text. Only ~24% of a direct-reading draft's statements have a counterpart in the reference, so the primary endpoint ignores most of what each strategy writes; the remainder is checked only by a same-family fidelity audit that does not test correctness, omissions or misattributed citations.

Single proprietary model, called through a CLI with no temperature or seed control; whether any conclusion (closeness of the reading strategies, case-table deficit) transfers to other model families, including open models, is untested. For a benchmark intended to compare system designs, at least one additional model family would substantially strengthen generality.

Strategies are the authors' own implementations rather than published systems (e.g., GraphRAG, PaperQA2-style agents), and some deficits are acknowledged to stem from implementation choices (extraction effort), which limits what the paradigm-level comparison can claim.

Several secondary/negative results are weak by construction or under-powered: recall-then-verify may not add content from the papers, so its low coverage is partly built in; variant precision for memory strategies rests on 23-30 entries; the learned curation guide is deliberately tiny; the planted-error test uses only blunt single-value substitutions and does not test omissions or citation errors.

Reusability as a benchmark is limited: curator text is not redistributed (only fact IDs and statuses), the full text set depends on open-access availability, and the scoring depends on the specific model's judgements, so others cannot easily reproduce the endpoint with a different judge without re-deriving the fact lists.

Presentation is very dense. Sections 4.2-4.4 pack many numbers, intervals and caveats into nearly every sentence, terminology (mean over entries vs pooled, stated/partly stated, compared entries, add-ons vs parents) takes effort to track, and the long title could be tightened. A clearer separation of headline findings from robustness checks would help readers.
Questions: Can you provide a human (curator or domain-expert) validation on even a small random sample (e.g., 200-300 facts) of (a) the fact-present/absent judgements, (b) the 'supplied text states the fact' judgements, and (c) audit verdicts, with agreement statistics? How would the Table 2 conclusions change under the observed error rates?

Have you re-run the judging (fact matching and 'stated' judgements) with a model from a different family to check for self-preference or same-model correlation, even if generation stays with one model?

Do the conclusions hold with a second generator model family (ideally an open-weights model)? If cost prevents a full rerun, a 30-entry subset with direct reading, evidence graph and case table first would already be informative.

How were the fixed fact lists produced and checked (granularity, deduplication, facts that are inferences rather than statements)? What is the variance in fact count per paragraph, and does per-entry averaging give entries with few facts undue weight?

Given that inputs fit in one prompt, do you expect any separation between direct reading and extraction/agentic strategies at larger reference counts? The 30-75 reference exploratory tier has only 10 compared entries; can you say more about it?

For case table first, how much of the residual deficit on full-text papers after matching is due to the per-patient schema discarding non-patient content (e.g., functional studies), which is common in OMIM allelic-variant text?
Facts conveyed but stated in no supplied text (24 of 1,458 for abstract/title-only papers): were these spot-checked for whether they were recalled from memory or are judge errors?
Limitations: The authors list their limitations clearly (single model family, no human validation, narrow reference, curator reference list supplied, open-access-only text, uneven stops, small-reference regime). The most important missing mitigation is any human validation of the judgements on which every result depends.

Generated entries are rightly framed as drafts for expert review rather than clinical guidance; the paper should also note that fidelity-audited text can still propagate source errors into a knowledge base.
